text: why don't I apply the same critical lens to the Book of Mormon that I do to the Bible hey everybody I'm Dan mclen I'm a
scholar of the Bible and religion and I've been seeing more and more people in my comment sections asking this rhetorical question and there are two
things to say by way of response the first is that the Book of Mormon is neither my academic specialization nor the subject of this channel I did spend
10 years as a scripture translation supervisor for the LDS church during which time I supervise many translations of the Book of Mormon into other
languages but my priority during that time and the reason I was hired was to help non-english speaking members of the church better access the Bible of the
five degrees that I hold one is a vocational degree in massage therapy and the other four are directly related to
cognitive Linguistics the cognitive science of religion the Hebrew Bible biblical studies or ancient near Eastern
studies my academic expertise is focused on the study of the Bible not the Book of Mormon but this brings up the second
thing to note and that is that I do apply the same critical lens to the Book of Mormon that I do to the Bible I have repeatedly and consistently on my
channel and in other social media appearances pointed out that the data do not support an ancient origin for the Book of Mormon and that if we want to
understand what it's saying we don't do that by back translating it into Mayan or Egyptian or Hebrew we do that by
situating it within in its early to mid 19th century literary and linguistic and rhetorical context and I have published
research doing precisely that this paper second Nephi 25:23 in literary and rhetorical context was published in 2020
in the Journal of Book of Mormon studies and in this paper I begin from that assertion that to best understand this
text we have to situate it within the rhetorical context into which it was published and I examined the end of this
passage which is a very famous one for Latter-Day Saints it says we know that it is by grace that we are saved after
all we can do historically that has long been interpreted by latterday Saints to mean that we have to do all we can do
before Grace kicks in and what I demonstrate in this paper is that that phrase after all we can do was quite common in the late 18th into the early
and mid 19th centuries and even within discussions about Grace and everywhere it occurs it is never used specifically
to mean following after in time it is always used to mean despite all we can do and particularly within those
discussions about Grace in other words when the Book of Mormon was first articulated and published everyone would
have understood this phrase to mean we are saved by grace despite all we can do not once we have done all we can do and
that overturns a longstanding and authoritative and very popular reading of this passage so hopefully that
assuages the concerns from any of those folks who have been sincerely wondering why I don't apply the same critical lens to the Book of Mormon that I do to the
Bible the reality is that I do and the fit for this video has been Rogue
